paras: The lynching of Henry Davis took place in the early morning of August 9, 1885, when a crowd of masked men broke into the jail at Cuthbert, Georgia, took out Davis, a 19-year-old Black man, and hanged and shot him at a nearby railroad bridge. Davis had been charged with assaulting Sylvia Knight, the nine-year-old daughter of a Baptist minister, two days earlier. The story ran in papers from Savannah to Dakota Territory, and white papers presented the killing as deserved punishment.

According to the Cuthbert dispatches, on Friday, August 7, Sylvia Knight and her seven-year-old brother were walking to school when a naked man seized the girl on the road and carried her into the woods. The children, who lived near Ward's Station, told their parents the attacker had a scar on his hip. Their father, the Rev. John T. Knight, and an armed posse of neighbors searched the woods and "made prisoners of five or six negroes on suspicion."

The captives were brought before the children, who were said to have picked out Davis, and a scar was found on his hip. The Dawson Journal added that Davis worked for Col. H. Crittenden of Ward's Station and was examined before a Dr. Bridgeman. A crowd of about a hundred men surrounded him and threatened to kill him on the spot, but the girl's father begged them to let the law take its course, and Davis was taken to the Cuthbert jail.

Before dawn on Sunday, August 9, about a hundred masked men armed with guns and revolvers gathered at the jail and demanded Davis; the Savannah Morning News put the hour at 2 a.m. and the Sun's wire at 4 a.m. The jailer refused, and the New-York Tribune's correspondent wrote that he "hid his keys and threatened to kill the first man who attacked his citadel." The crowd forced the doors with improvised battering rams, broke into Davis's cell, and quieted his resistance with revolvers held to his head.

Davis was then led to a railroad bridge nearby and hanged from it, by a slip-noose over a sill in the Savannah account and with a plough line in the Tribune's. Before he had strangled, the men fired a volley into his body.

No report of an inquest, arrest or grand jury inquiry appears in the coverage found. A week later the Savannah Morning News reported that a traveling salesman in Lumpkin carried a piece of the rope in his vest pocket and said "it beats a rabbit foot for luck."

The first wire brief, printed in Grand Rapids and New Haven on August 10, reported only that a mob had tried to lynch Davis and had been talked out of it by the girl's father. The same day, fuller Cuthbert dispatches in the Savannah Morning News, the New York Sun and the New-York Tribune reported the hanging, and a Chicago Tribune special carrying the Sun's text ran in the Omaha Daily Bee the next day under the headline "Georgia Justice." A two-line Atlanta Constitution special appeared in the St. Paul Daily Globe, the Salt Lake Herald and other western papers, and the Washington Evening Star reprinted the full wire.

Headlines endorsed the killing: the Sun called it "The People Settled with Him," and the Springfield Globe-Republic put the brief under "Deservedly Lynched." The Savannah paper described the alleged crime as "one of the most revolting ever perpetrated in this county" and called the lynchers "masked avengers," while the nearby Dawson Journal headed its account "A Demon's Deed" and closed that Davis "met a quick and deserved fate." Distant weeklies reduced the case to a single sentence in crime columns, one of them garbling the names to "Harry Davis" and "Miss Minnie Gordon."

Accounts differ on the size and timing of the mob: the wire reports gave about a hundred men in the early morning of August 9, while the Dawson Journal said "sixty or seventy-five citizens" broke Davis out on Saturday night. Papers also named the charge variously as an "assault," an "outrage" and "rape."

bases: About 100 masked, armed men broke into the Cuthbert jail, took out Henry Davis, a Black prisoner charged with assaulting a white child, and hanged and shot him at a railroad bridge (A3, A4, A5).

Davis was killed by a masked crowd of 100 (or 60 to 75) men who overpowered the jailer and took him from custody without any lawful authority (A3, A5, A16); they acted on the charge that he had assaulted a nine-year-old white girl, and the press called it 'Georgia justice' and a 'deserved fate' (A11, A16).

Separate Cuthbert dispatches to the Savannah Morning News, the New-York Tribune and the Chicago Tribune/Sun wire, the Constitution brief, and the Dawson Journal agree that Davis was taken from jail and hanged and shot at a railroad bridge (A3, A4, A5, A7, A16).

accounts.gist: Davis was captured and a mob tried to lynch him, but the girl's father begged it to let the law take its course and it agreed; the girl's condition was critical.

accounts.label: Cuthbert wire reports
accounts.gist: About 100 masked men broke into the jail before dawn on August 9, overpowered the jailer, and hanged Davis at a railroad bridge, shooting him before he strangled.

accounts.label: Dawson Journal (regional weekly)
accounts.gist: Davis was identified by the girl among half a dozen arrested men and examined by Dr. Bridgeman; 'sixty or seventy-five citizens' broke him out of jail Saturday night, hanged and shot him.

framing.detail: Headlines 'The People Settled with Him', 'Georgia Justice' and 'Deservedly Lynched' presented the lynching as rightful punishment.
The Savannah Morning News called the mob 'masked avengers' and the alleged assault 'one of the most revolting ever perpetrated in this county'.
The Dawson Journal headed its story 'A Demon's Deed' and called the lynching 'a quick and deserved fate'.
Distant papers ran the Constitution brief or the full wire as a one-line or one-paragraph item without comment.

conflicts.note: All fall within the night of August 8-9; the Cuthbert dispatches dated August 9 place it early Sunday morning.
The 100 figure is the wire's; the Dawson Journal is a nearby weekly writing four days later.
The Union County Courier brief describes the same Cuthbert jail-and-bridge lynching; the names look garbled rather than a second case.
